title: Statistics Seminar
text:
Lab Protocol



Equip the lab. We start together: in the first meetings, we learn how to build Monte Carlo simulations and use them to make statistical methods fail (1  Monte Carlo Simulations: The Laboratory).

Assign the specimens. Together, we allocate the topics, one statistical method per lab group (2  Topics: The Specimens).

Dissect it. Work out its assumptions, its mechanics, and how it turns on its users, and write it all down in your seminar thesis (3  Writing the Seminar Thesis).

Present it. Show your creature to the seminar, including the moment it turns on you.


Lab Rules

You work in lab groups of three.

Grading:

80% seminar thesis, your written lab report
20% presentation, where every group member speaks. Victor abandoned his creature; you stand by yours.

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
2.1 Instrumental Variables
In the linear model \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + u_i\), the OLS estimator is inconsistent if the regressor \(X_i\) is endogenous, i.e., \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_i, u_i) \neq 0\), for instance due to omitted variables, measurement error, or simultaneity. Instrumental variables (IV) estimators, such as two-stage least squares (2SLS), use an instrument \(Z_i\) to isolate the exogenous variation in \(X_i\).
Literature: Angrist and Pischke (2009, Ch. 4), Staiger and Stock (1997), Stock, Wright, and Yogo (2002)

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
Relevance: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i, X_i) \neq 0\)
Exogeneity: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i, u_i) = 0\) 




Weak instruments: If \(Z_i\) is only weakly correlated with \(X_i\), 2SLS is biased towards OLS, its distribution is far from normal, and \(t\)-tests reject far too often.
Invalid instruments: A small correlation between \(Z_i\) and \(u_i\) can cause a large inconsistency, especially when the instrument is weak.
Many instruments: Adding more and more instruments can make 2SLS behave like OLS.

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
2.2 Heteroskedasticity-Robust Standard Errors
In the linear regression model \(Y_i = X_i'\beta + u_i\), the classical OLS standard errors assume homoskedastic errors, \(\operatorname{Var}(u_i \mid X_i) = \sigma^2\). If the error variance depends on \(X_i\), these standard errors are wrong, and so are the resulting \(t\)-tests and confidence intervals. Heteroskedasticity-robust (“sandwich”) standard errors, such as HC0 to HC3, remain valid under heteroskedasticity of unknown form.


Random sampling of \((Y_i, X_i)\)
Exogeneity: \(E(u_i \mid X_i) = 0\)
Finite fourth moments; no perfect multicollinearity
Validity is asymptotic, i.e., for large \(n\)




Classical standard errors under heteroskedasticity: How far off are the size of \(t\)-tests and the coverage of confidence intervals?
Small samples: HC0 tends to underestimate the variance, so robust \(t\)-tests reject too often. Do HC2 and HC3 fix this?
Leverage points: A few observations with extreme \(X_i\) values can make robust standard errors very unreliable.


Literature: White (1980), MacKinnon and White (1985), Long and Ervin (2000)

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
2.3 Nonparametric Density Estimation
How do we estimate the density \(f\) of a random variable \(X\) without assuming a parametric family such as the normal distribution? The kernel density estimator \[
\hat{f}_h(x) = \frac{1}{nh} \sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x - X_i}{h}\right)
\] places a small “bump” \(K\) (the kernel) at each observation and averages them. The bandwidth \(h\) controls how smooth the estimate is.


\(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are i.i.d. with density \(f\)
\(f\) is smooth (e.g., twice continuously differentiable)
\(h \to 0\) and \(nh \to \infty\) as \(n \to \infty\)




Bandwidth choice: Too small, and you see spurious bumps; too large, and real modes vanish. Rules of thumb, such as Silverman’s, can oversmooth multimodal densities.
Boundaries: For densities with bounded support (e.g., an exponential distribution), the estimator is biased near the boundary.
Dimensions: In more than a few dimensions, the required sample size explodes (curse of dimensionality).
Dependent data: What happens to bandwidth selection if the observations are not independent?


Literature: Silverman (1986), Wand and Jones (1995)

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
2.4 Nonparametric Regression
How do we estimate the regression function \(m(x) = E(Y \mid X = x)\) without assuming that it is linear, or of any other parametric form? Kernel regression estimators fit a local average (Nadaraya–Watson) or a local straight line (local linear) around each point \(x\), weighting observations by a kernel \(K\) with bandwidth \(h\). The Nadaraya–Watson estimator is \[
\hat{m}_h(x) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x - X_i}{h}\right) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x - X_i}{h}\right)}.
\]


\((Y_1, X_1), \dots, (Y_n, X_n)\) are i.i.d.
\(m\) is smooth (e.g., twice continuously differentiable), and the density of \(X\) is bounded away from zero
\(h \to 0\) and \(nh \to \infty\) as \(n \to \infty\)




Bandwidth choice: How sensitive are the results to \(h\)? How well does cross-validation work?
Boundaries: Nadaraya–Watson is biased near the boundary of the support of \(X\). Does local linear regression fix this?
Sparse designs: What happens in regions with only few \(X_i\) values?
Dimensions: With several regressors, the curse of dimensionality strikes again.


Literature: Fan and Gijbels (1996), Li and Racine (2007, Ch. 2)

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
2.5 Multiple Testing
If you carry out \(m\) tests, each at level \(\alpha = 0.05\), then you should expect about \(0.05 \cdot m\) false rejections even if all null hypotheses are true. Multiple testing procedures control either the family-wise error rate (FWER), i.e., the probability of at least one false rejection (Bonferroni, Holm), or the false discovery rate (FDR), i.e., the expected proportion of false rejections among all rejections (Benjamini–Hochberg).


Valid \(p\)-values for each individual test
Bonferroni and Holm: no assumptions on the dependence between the tests
Benjamini–Hochberg: independent (or positively dependent) test statistics




No correction: How quickly do false discoveries pile up as \(m\) grows?
Power: How much power do Bonferroni and Holm lose compared to Benjamini–Hochberg, and how does this depend on the number of false null hypotheses?
Dependence: Does Benjamini–Hochberg still control the FDR if the test statistics are negatively correlated?


Literature: Holm (1979), Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001)

title: 2  Topics: The Specimens
text:
2.6 Rank-Based Tests
The \(t\)-test assumes normally distributed data, or a sample large enough for the central limit theorem to work. Rank-based tests, such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney rank-sum test, replace the observations by their ranks. This makes them robust to outliers and heavy tails, and they lose surprisingly little power when the data are in fact normal.


Independent observations (within and between samples)
Continuous distributions (no ties)
Rank-sum test: under the null hypothesis, both samples come from the same distribution




What does it test? The rank-sum test is often sold as a test for equal medians. Is it? Simulate two distributions with equal medians but different variances or shapes, and check the size.
Heavy tails: How do the \(t\)-test and the rank-sum test compare under normal, \(t\)-distributed, and contaminated data?
Ties: What happens with discrete data, e.g., Likert scales?


Literature: Hollander, Wolfe, and Chicken (2014), Fagerland and Sandvik (2009)




Angrist, Joshua D., and Jörn-Steffen Pischke. 2009. Mostly Harmless Econometrics: An Empiricist’s Companion. Princeton University Press.


Benjamini, Yoav, and Yosef Hochberg. 1995. “Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 57 (1): 289–300.


Benjamini, Yoav, and Daniel Yekutieli. 2001. “The Control of the False Discovery Rate in Multiple Testing Under Dependency.” The Annals of Statistics 29 (4): 1165–88.


Fagerland, Morten W., and Leiv Sandvik. 2009. “The Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney Test Under Scrutiny.” Statistics in Medicine 28 (10): 1487–97.


Fan, Jianqing, and Irène Gijbels. 1996. Local Polynomial Modelling and Its Applications. Chapman & Hall.


Hollander, Myles, Douglas A. Wolfe, and Eric Chicken. 2014. Nonparametric Statistical Methods. 3rd ed. Wiley.


Holm, Sture. 1979. “A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure.” Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6 (2): 65–70.


Li, Qi, and Jeffrey S. Racine. 2007. Nonparametric Econometrics: Theory and Practice. Princeton University Press.

MacKinnon, James G., and Halbert White. 1985. “Some Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimators with Improved Finite Sample Properties.” Journal of Econometrics 29 (3): 305–25.

Staiger, Douglas, and James H. Stock. 1997. “Instrumental Variables Regression with Weak Instruments.” Econometrica 65 (3): 557–86.


Stock, James H., Jonathan H. Wright, and Motohiro Yogo. 2002. “A Survey of Weak Instruments and Weak Identification in Generalized Method of Moments.” Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 20 (4): 518–29.

title: 3  Writing the Seminar Thesis
text:
State the statistical model and all assumptions under which the method is justified.



Describe the setting: What kind of data? What is the parameter of interest \(\theta\)?
State the assumptions precisely, e.g., i.i.d. sampling, moment conditions, distributional assumptions, model specification, sample size requirements.
For each assumption, explain in words what it means and why the method needs it. Where in the derivation or proof is it used?
Discuss whether the assumptions are plausible in typical applications.

title: 3  Writing the Seminar Thesis
section: 3.2 The Organs: How the Method Works
text:
3.2 The Organs: How the Method Works

Explain the mechanics of the method: the estimator, test, or algorithm and its theoretical properties.



Define the method formally and give the intuition behind it.
State the main theoretical results (e.g., unbiasedness, consistency, asymptotic distribution, size and power of a test) and explain where the assumptions enter.
Use a simple example to illustrate how the method works.

title: 3  Writing the Seminar Thesis
section: 3.3 The Spark: Bringing It to Life in Code
text:
3.3 The Spark: Bringing It to Life in Code

Implement the method and apply it, so that the reader sees it working.



Show how to apply the method in R or Python. Implementing core parts yourself is the best way to understand them.
Apply the method to a (real or simulated) data example and interpret the results carefully.

title: 3  Writing the Seminar Thesis
section: 3.4 When It Turns on You: Failure Investigations
text:
3.4 When It Turns on You: Failure Investigations

Use Monte Carlo simulations to investigate when the method works, and how it fails when its assumptions are violated.

This is the core of your thesis. Design your simulation study like an experiment:


Baseline. Start with a data generating process under which all assumptions hold. Check that the method behaves as the theory predicts.
Violate one assumption at a time. Change the data generating process so that exactly one assumption breaks (e.g., heavy tails, heteroskedasticity, dependence, misspecification, small samples). This way, you know which assumption is responsible for a failure.
Vary the severity. Let the violation range from mild to severe, and vary the sample size \(n\). Does the failure vanish as \(n\) grows, or does it persist?
Measure the damage. Choose performance measures that fit your method, for instance:

estimators: bias, variance, and mean squared error,
confidence intervals: coverage probability and average length,
tests: empirical size and power.

Make it reproducible. Use enough Monte Carlo replications, set a random seed, and include your code.
Report clearly. Summarize the results in tables and plots, and interpret them: When can a user safely rely on the method? What warning signs should a user look for in practice?

title: 3  Writing the Seminar Thesis
text:
3.5 Formalities

Length: 15–20 pages main text, including figures and tables; excluding title page, table of contents, references, and appendix.
Format: 12 pt font, 1.5 line spacing, 2.5 cm margins, submitted as a PDF.
Code: Code does not belong in the main text. Show only short snippets that help the reader understand the method. Submit your full code separately, such that all results can be reproduced (fixed random seed).
Submission: thesis.pdf and a ZIP file with your complete thesis folder (text, code, and literature).
Submission deadline: TBA


Thesis Template
Download the Quarto thesis template. It already implements all formal requirements and renders to PDF. It also shows how to keep code out of the PDF: the method is implemented in R/functions.R, the simulation study in R/simulation.R, and thesis.qmd only reads the saved simulation results to show tables and figures. See the included README.md for details.
